result:
The best thing I ever saw in a museum was a small boy explaining a revolving door to his grandfather. They hadn’t bought tickets yet. As far as the boy was concerned, they were already at the exhibit.

“You have to keep walking,” he said.

His grandfather, who had probably been through several thousand revolving doors, gave it a look of reasonable doubt. “Even when I get outside?”

The boy considered this. “No. Outside you can do what you want.”

They went around twice. On the second revolution the grandfather raised a hand to the woman at the ticket desk, as if passing her on a riverboat. She raised hers back.

I spent the next hour looking at Roman glass. There was a little blue cup I liked very much, repaired from three pieces, with a thumbnail-sized chip missing from the rim. The label said it had been used for drinking. Usually that kind of information slides right off me, but that morning I could picture somebody owning it: turning the chipped side away from a guest, filling it a little short of the top.

On my way out I took the revolving door around twice. The woman at the desk was on the phone by then. She waved anyway.
